question: My 17-year-old daughter has frequent heavy nosebleeds and wants to start donating. What decides on the day whether she's allowed?
answer: She can be accepted if she passes the haemoglobin screening test.

question: Is it okay to give blood while I'm on a course of Tamiflu?
answer: Only if you're taking it as prevention, haven't been told to stay at home and have had no flu symptoms; not if it's treating flu.

question: I'm taking Tamiflu as a precaution because my flatmate has flu, but three days ago I had a temperature of 38.5 and a cough. Can I donate?
answer: No, having flu symptoms in the 7 days before or while taking oseltamivir means you must not donate.

question: My GP gave me a cortisone jab in my worn-out knee five days ago. How soon can I give blood?
answer: Not yet; you need to wait at least 7 days after a steroid joint injection given in the NHS or by a qualified professional.

question: I paid privately for a PRP injection into my arthritic hip two months ago, given by a qualified doctor. Is there still a wait before I can donate?
answer: Yes, you must wait at least 4 months after an autologous platelet-rich plasma joint injection.

question: I had an infection in the bone of my leg and finished the antibiotics last spring. How long do I have to wait to give blood?
answer: You must wait 24 months from completing treatment and being cured.

question: My osteomyelitis was declared cured and treatment stopped 18 months ago. Am I eligible to donate now?
answer: No, you need to wait until 24 months after completing treatment and cure.

question: A scan showed my bones are getting a bit thin, so I take calcium and vitamin D. Will that stop me being a donor?
answer: No, you can donate if the underlying cause isn't itself a reason to defer, even while on preventive treatment other than denosumab.

question: I have a Prolia injection every six months for low bone density. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: No, treatment with the monoclonal antibody denosumab (Prolia) means you must not donate.

question: My dad has a bone disorder that's made his pelvis thick and misshapen, and he takes painkillers for the ache. Can he still donate?
answer: Yes, he can be accepted even on painkillers or bisphosphonates, provided he's otherwise fit.

question: I'm 58 with Paget's disease and take a bisphosphonate tablet every week. Does the medication rule me out from giving blood?
answer: No, you can be accepted even while taking bisphosphonates.

question: I take co-codamol most days. Does that automatically mean I can't give blood?
answer: No, the type of medication doesn't matter if you're otherwise fit; the reason you take it is what gets assessed.

question: I'm prescribed tramadol for an old rugby injury that's healed but still aches. Would I be turned away from donating?
answer: No, you can be accepted if you're otherwise fit to donate, whatever the painkiller.

question: Sometimes my heart flutters and pounds when I'm stressed. Is giving blood still an option for me?
answer: Only if your GP has ruled out a heart cause, you're not having investigations and you're symptom-free on the day.

question: My GP checked out my racing heartbeat, found nothing wrong with my heart and started me on propranolol to stop the episodes. I feel fine today. Can I donate?
answer: Yes, you can be accepted even on beta blockers since a cardiac cause has been excluded and you're symptom-free.

question: I had a small non-cancerous lump removed from one of the calcium-controlling glands in my neck and I'm fully recovered. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, if you're well, have recovered from surgery for a benign adenoma and aren't under specialist follow-up.

question: I have primary hyperparathyroidism; my calcium has been steady for 18 months with no symptoms and no treatment. Could I become a platelet donor?
answer: No, you can be accepted for whole blood donation only, not component donation.

question: I caught slapped cheek from my kids last month. When can I go back to giving blood?
answer: Once it is more than 4 weeks since you recovered from the feverish symptoms (and from any positive test).

question: My fever and sore throat from parvovirus went five weeks ago, but my wrists still ache and there's a faint rash on my arms. Am I okay to donate?
answer: Yes, it's over 4 weeks since recovery and lingering joint pain or rash doesn't prevent donation.

question: My little boy has just come down with slapped cheek from nursery. Do I need to put off giving blood?
answer: Yes, wait 3 weeks from your last contact unless you've definitely had it before or the contact was only after his rash appeared.

question: My niece stayed with us ten days ago while she had a temperature, before her face went red with fifth disease. I've never had it myself. Can I donate this week?
answer: No, it is less than 3 weeks since contact with her during the infectious phase.

question: I had a bleeding sore in my stomach lining a while back and still take omeprazole every day to stop it coming back. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: Yes, if you have no recent symptoms you can donate even on maintenance treatment.

question: I'm two weeks into a course of tablets to heal a duodenal ulcer. Can I donate this weekend?
answer: No, you must not donate while on active treatment to heal an ulcer.

question: Is it alright to give blood while I'm on my time of the month?
answer: Yes, you can donate during a period, though it makes iron deficiency more likely.

question: My period is two weeks late, but a pregnancy test was negative and I feel perfectly well. Can I still donate?
answer: Yes, a missed period is acceptable if pregnancy has been excluded and you are well.

question: As a child I had a hip problem where the top of my thigh bone lost its blood supply and flattened. Does that matter for giving blood now?
answer: No, you can be accepted.

question: I had surgery for Perthes disease when I was eight and now have mild arthritis in that hip. Am I eligible to donate?
answer: Yes, you can be accepted, though any painkillers you take may affect whether your donation is used for platelets.

question: I've got a benign growth on the gland at the base of my brain that makes too much prolactin, and I take cabergoline for it. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, if it's confirmed non-malignant and you have no symptoms, you can be accepted even on oral medication.

question: Two years ago surgeons removed my pituitary tumour through my nose, and everything has healed. Is that a barrier to donating?
answer: No, after trans-sphenoidal surgery for a pituitary tumour you can be accepted once all wounds are healed.

question: A blood test at my GP showed my clotting cells were a bit low and they're looking into why. Should I hold off giving blood?
answer: Yes, you must not donate while under investigation for an abnormal platelet count.

question: My platelet count was high, but the haematologist found no underlying cause and discharged me with no follow-up. Can I donate now?
answer: Yes, if no cause leading to deferral was found and no monitoring or follow-up is needed, you can be accepted.

question: I bruise really easily and was told I was born with clotting cells that don't work properly. Can I be a blood donor?
answer: No, people with an inherited platelet disorder must not donate.

question: Family screening showed I carry Glanzmann's thrombasthenia, but I've never had any bleeding symptoms and my platelet function tests came back normal. Is there any chance I could donate?
answer: Possibly; an unaffected carrier who meets all other criteria must be referred to a Designated Clinical Support Officer.

question: My lung suddenly collapsed for no reason last year (I'm tall and skinny), but I'm completely better now. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, once recovered it doesn't stop you donating unless it was linked to cystic fibrosis or emphysema.

question: My lung collapsed on its own because of my emphysema; it's re-inflated now and I'm home from hospital. Am I able to donate?
answer: No, a spontaneous pneumothorax associated with emphysema means you must not donate.

question: I punctured a lung when I broke my ribs in a car crash. How do they decide when I can start giving blood?
answer: A collapsed lung caused by injury is assessed under the Accident entry.

question: Falling off a ladder cracked my ribs and collapsed my lung six months ago; I've healed fully. Does the collapsed lung stop me donating?
answer: A traumatic pneumothorax is assessed under the Accident guidance rather than as a lung condition.

question: I inherited cysts on my kidneys from my mum. My kidneys work normally and I only see my GP about it. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, if kidney function is normal, there's no high blood pressure, no anaemia from it, no treatment and only GP monitoring.

question: I have polycystic kidneys and my doctor started me on ramipril to protect them, even though my blood pressure is normal. Does that rule me out?
answer: Yes, requiring any treatment, including preventive blood pressure medication, means you must not donate.

question: At my last session they said my blood count was too high and sent me away. Will I ever be able to come back?
answer: Only if specialist tests rule out polycythaemia vera or other causes and no treatment or further investigation is planned; then whole blood or double red cell donation is possible.

question: I use testosterone gel and my doctor suggested giving blood to bring my haematocrit down. Will the blood service accept me for that?
answer: No, donation must not be used to manage medication-related polycythaemia; you should be deferred and advised to see your health provider.

question: I've got polycystic ovaries and take metformin for it. Am I still allowed to donate blood?
answer: Yes, the diagnosis and its usual medication don't prevent donation if you're eligible under the entries for any related problems.

question: I have PCOS and my dermatologist has prescribed finasteride for excess facial hair. Can I keep giving blood?
answer: No, finasteride is a treatment that specifically precludes donation, even though the condition itself doesn't.

question: I've got a rare genetic condition affecting how my body makes the red pigment in blood, which gives me painful attacks. Does that stop me from donating?
answer: Usually yes; only the acute types are acceptable, and only if it's 12 months or more since the last attack with no current skin lesions.

question: I have variegate porphyria; my last acute attack was eight months ago and my skin is clear. Can I donate now?
answer: No, you must wait until 12 months since your last acute attack.

question: I stopped the daily pills from the sexual health clinic that protect you against the AIDS virus two months ago. How much longer until I can start giving blood?
answer: You must wait until more than 3 months since your last oral PrEP or PEP, provided there's no other blood safety risk.

question: My last cabotegravir injection for HIV prevention was 14 months ago. Am I eligible to donate yet?
answer: No, you must wait more than 2 years after the last PrEP injection.

question: I had my baby five months ago and I'm still breastfeeding. Could I give blood yet?
answer: Not yet; you must wait 6 months after delivery, but breastfeeding itself doesn't stop you after that.

question: I had an early miscarriage at nine weeks without much bleeding; follow-up is finished and I didn't need methotrexate. Is there still a long wait before I can donate?
answer: No, a pregnancy ending before 12 weeks without significant blood loss can be accepted once follow-up is complete, if a clinical support physician agrees.

question: Two of my blood relatives died of CJD. Does that mean I'm barred from giving blood?
answer: Yes, unless genetic counselling has told you you're not at risk, confirmed by a Designated Clinical Support Officer.

question: Years ago I got a letter from the hospital saying I might be at higher risk of CJD because of instruments used in my operation. Can I donate?
answer: No, anyone told they've been put at increased risk of prion disease from surgery must not donate.

question: I had some inflammation of my back passage that settled down by itself without any treatment. Is it fine for me to give blood?
answer: Yes, if the cause doesn't exclude you and you're not on treatment, you can be accepted.

question: I'm currently using suppositories my GP prescribed for proctitis. Should I still go to my donation appointment this week?
answer: No, proctitis requiring treatment means you must not donate.

question: I'm 65 and take tamsulosin because I keep needing to get up at night to pee. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, benign prostate problems treated only with alpha blockers are acceptable.

question: My PSA came back high and my GP has referred me to urology for further tests. Am I okay to donate while I wait?
answer: No, being referred to a specialist for a high PSA means you must not donate.

question: I've got a few mild scaly patches on my elbows that I just put cream on. Does that stop me giving blood?
answer: No, if it's mild, the needle site is unaffected and you use only topical treatment, you can donate.

question: I stopped taking acitretin for my psoriasis two years ago. Is that long enough before donating?
answer: No, you must wait 36 months from the last dose of acitretin.

question: I had a high temperature last week but I haven't been abroad and feel fine now. How long should I leave it before giving blood?
answer: Wait 2 weeks from the episode of fever, unless it was due to a cold you're recovering from.

question: Four days ago I had a temperature of 38.4 with a stinking cold, and I'm on the mend now. Can I still donate tomorrow?
answer: Yes, a fever from a common cold that you're recovering from is acceptable.

question: I came down with a fever while on safari in Kenya last month. Does that affect when I can give blood?
answer: A fever linked to travel is assessed under the travel-related entries such as Malaria and the Geographical Disease Risk Index.

question: I had a temperature of 38.5 after getting back from the USA during the season when West Nile virus was circulating. Which rules decide when I can donate?
answer: A travel-related fever is assessed under the West Nile Virus and other travel-related entries.

question: If someone catches the deadly virus spread by bites from infected dogs and bats and somehow survives, can they ever give blood?
answer: Yes, anyone diagnosed with rabies must not donate, even if recovered.

question: I developed rabies after a dog bite in India, was treated in hospital and recovered three years ago. Am I eligible to donate now?
answer: No, a diagnosis of rabies means you must not donate even after recovery.

question: A stray dog bit me in Thailand and I had a course of emergency jabs against the virus it might carry. How long until I'm allowed to give blood?
answer: At least 12 months after the exposure, and only once your treating doctor has fully cleared you.

question: Eight months ago a bat scratched me in Peru; I had post-exposure vaccines and immunoglobulin, and my doctor has signed me off. Can I donate now?
answer: No, you must wait until at least 12 months after the exposure.

question: Before going backpacking I had jabs against the virus you can catch from dog bites, just as a precaution. Does that stop me giving blood?
answer: No, if you haven't been exposed to rabies you can be accepted.

question: I'm a vet nurse and had a routine rabies booster last week; I haven't been bitten or scratched by anything. Is it okay to donate on Friday?
answer: Yes, rabies immunisation without exposure is acceptable.

question: I had radiotherapy on a basal cell skin cancer on my nose, and the clinic has discharged me. Am I able to give blood?
answer: Yes, if all treatment is complete, you're discharged from follow-up and you're eligible under the Malignancy entry.

question: I had radiotherapy last year for keloid scars, which aren't cancerous, and I've fully recovered. Would I be accepted as a donor?
answer: It must be referred to a Designated Clinical Support Officer, as radiation for non-malignant conditions needs individual assessment.

question: I had a scan last week where they injected a radioactive tracer into my arm. Does that affect giving blood?
answer: It needs referral to a Designated Clinical Support Officer, although diagnostic tracers are usually cleared within 24 hours.

question: Four months ago I had radioactive iodine for an overactive thyroid. Can I give blood yet?
answer: No, you must wait at least 6 months after radioactive iodine for a non-malignant condition.

question: My fingers go white and numb whenever it's cold, and I take nifedipine to help. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, if it isn't part of an autoimmune condition, even while taking vasodilators.

question: My cold, white finger attacks turned out to be caused by scleroderma. Where does that leave me for donating?
answer: Because it's part of an autoimmune process, eligibility is decided under the Autoimmune disease entry.

question: I get puffed out just climbing one flight of stairs. Should I really be giving blood?
answer: No, being out of breath on minimal exertion means you must not donate.

question: I have bronchiectasis but haven't had a chest infection for several months. Am I allowed to donate?
answer: No, bronchiectasis counts as chronic infection and you must not donate.

question: Years ago a strep throat led to an illness that made my joints swell up, but a scan showed my heart wasn't damaged. Is giving blood okay for me?
answer: Yes, provided it's more than 24 months since symptoms stopped and there's no permanent heart valve damage.

question: My rheumatic fever symptoms ended 20 months ago and my heart scan was normal. Can I donate now?
answer: No, you must wait until 24 months after symptoms stopped.

question: I had a short-lived inflammatory illness with swollen glands in my chest and painful red lumps on my shins, which cleared up on its own. When could I give blood?
answer: Once it's more than 5 years since full recovery and finishing any treatment.

question: My acute sarcoidosis settled after a short course of steroids that ended four years ago. Am I eligible to donate?
answer: No, you need more than 5 years since finishing all treatment and full recovery.

question: I've had a long-term inflammatory condition causing little clumps of cells in my lungs for years, and I see a chest specialist annually. Is there any way I can give blood?
answer: No, people with chronic sarcoidosis must not donate.

question: My sarcoidosis has been chronic for six years but is currently stable without any medication. Would I be accepted?
answer: No, chronic sarcoidosis means you must not donate, even if stable and untreated.

question: I picked up an infection from sex and finished my antibiotics a few weeks ago. When am I allowed to give blood again?
answer: Check for a specific entry for the infection; otherwise wait 3 months from completing treatment.

question: I was treated for gonorrhoea and the course finished ten weeks ago. Can I donate yet?
answer: No, you must wait until 3 months after completing treatment.

question: My partner has just been diagnosed with chlamydia. Do I have to stop giving blood?
answer: No, if you aren't having treatment or investigations yourself you can be accepted.

question: My girlfriend was treated for gonorrhoea; I didn't need any treatment myself and we last had sex two months ago. Is there still a wait before I donate?
answer: Yes, you must wait until 3 months after your last sexual contact with her.

question: I used to get paid for sex but stopped about a year ago. Am I allowed to give blood now?
answer: Yes, you can be accepted once 3 or more months have passed since you last received money or drugs for sex.

question: Six weeks ago I swapped sex for drugs. How long after that do I have to wait to donate?
answer: You must wait until at least 3 months have passed since you last received drugs or money for sex.

question: I wear a Libre sensor on my arm to keep track of my sugar levels. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, if the reason for using it doesn't stop you donating and there's no inflammation or infection around the sensor.

question: I have a spinal cord stimulator implanted for nerve pain; the wound healed months ago and the pain condition itself isn't a problem for donating. Am I eligible?
answer: Yes, an implanted neuromodulator is acceptable once the site is fully healed and the underlying reason doesn't preclude donation.

question: I carry the gene for the blood disorder my brother has, where red cells change shape, but I'm not ill myself. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, you can usually donate, but your blood will be used for adults only.

question: I have sickle cell trait. Could my whole blood donation end up being given to a newborn baby?
answer: No, it isn't suitable for intrauterine or neonatal use and is accepted for adult use only.

question: I've got athlete's foot and use a cream from the chemist on it. Does that stop me giving blood?
answer: No, a superficial fungal infection treated only with local therapy is acceptable.

question: My partner has scabies, but I haven't got any itching or rash myself. Is it alright for me to donate?
answer: Yes, contact with scabies without being obviously infected is acceptable.

question: I snore badly and stop breathing in my sleep, so I wear a CPAP mask at night. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: Yes, if symptoms are well controlled, there is no daytime sleepiness or driving restriction, and no excluding underlying cause.

question: I have sleep apnoea and still nod off during the day, and the DVLA has told me to stop driving. Can I donate?
answer: No, donors with daytime sleepiness or a driving restriction must not donate.

question: I had the army's live pox vaccine three weeks ago and the scab on my arm still hasn't come off. Am I OK to give blood?
answer: No, not until the vaccination site has fully healed and at least 8 weeks have passed.

question: I was vaccinated against smallpox five weeks ago and the injection site has completely healed. Is there still a waiting period before I can donate?
answer: Yes, you must wait until at least 8 weeks after the inoculation.

question: I live with someone who just had the military's live pox jab. I haven't come out in any spots or blisters. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, a close contact with no new skin lesions can be accepted.

question: Six weeks ago a sore appeared on my hand after I touched my partner's smallpox vaccination site. It has healed now. Can I donate?
answer: No, you must wait until at least 8 weeks after the secondary sore appeared.

question: I get through about ten cigarettes a day. Does that rule me out of being a blood donor?
answer: No, smokers can donate.

question: I'm a heavy smoker with an appointment next week. Will I be able to light up at the session while I'm waiting?
answer: You can donate as a smoker, but all donation sessions are no-smoking by law.

question: I'm wearing nicotine patches to help me quit cigarettes. Is it still fine for me to give blood?
answer: Yes, if you are well and not having side effects from the treatment.

question: I started Champix last week to stop smoking and it's making me feel sick and light-headed. Should I keep my donation appointment tomorrow?
answer: No, you must not donate while experiencing symptoms related to the treatment.

question: I was diagnosed with Chagas disease years ago when I lived in Bolivia. Is giving blood in the UK off the table for me?
answer: Yes, anyone who has ever had the infection cannot donate whole blood or platelets.

question: I had Chagas infection treated with tablets in Brazil and the doctors there said I was cured. Can I donate whole blood now?
answer: No, there is no certain cure, so anyone ever infected must not donate whole blood or platelets.

question: My mum was born in Colombia but I was born and raised in Leeds. Does her birthplace make any difference to me giving blood?
answer: Yes, you can only donate whole blood if a validated T. cruzi antibody test is negative.

question: I spent six weeks working on a small family farm in rural Peru and got home three months ago. Can I give whole blood?
answer: Not yet, you need at least 4 months since the last exposure and a negative T. cruzi antibody test.

question: I had Chagas once. Would I be able to give plasma instead of whole blood?
answer: No, anyone who has ever been infected cannot donate, even plasma for fractionation.

question: I'm booked for plasma-only donation. I once had a positive Chagas antibody result and took benznidazole, and I've been told I'm clear. Can I donate plasma?
answer: No, people who have ever been infected with T. cruzi must not donate plasma either.

question: I grew up in Guatemala. If I only give plasma, is my background a problem?
answer: No, plasma-only donors can be accepted without applying the Chagas risk rules.

question: I lived on a rural farm in Bolivia for three months and got back two weeks ago. I only donate plasma for fractionation. Do I need a Chagas antibody test first?
answer: No, accept; T. cruzi antibody testing is not required for plasma-for-fractionation donors.

question: I was born with an opening in my spine and have a drain tube fitted in my head. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: No, a person with an indwelling shunt must not donate.

question: I have spina bifida and last used a catheter to empty my bladder three days ago. Can I donate today?
answer: No, you must wait at least 7 days after catheterisation.

question: I had my spleen taken out after a car crash and now take penicillin every day. Can I still be a blood donor?
answer: Yes, if it was removed because of injury and you have recovered, even on preventive antibiotics.

question: My spleen was removed three years ago to treat ITP and I've been well ever since. Am I eligible to donate?
answer: No, after removal for immune thrombocytopenia you need at least 5 years from recovery.

question: I use a brown preventer inhaler every morning and night for my asthma. Does that stop me giving blood?
answer: No, using a steroid inhaler for prevention is acceptable.

question: I finished a five-day course of prednisolone tablets for an asthma flare-up four days ago. How soon can I donate?
answer: You must wait until at least 7 days after finishing the oral steroid course.

question: I've had a bag on my tummy since an accident damaged my bowel, and it's all healthy now. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, if the reason for it does not itself exclude you and the stoma is healthy.

question: My husband had an ileostomy created during his operation for bowel cancer. Is he allowed to donate?
answer: No, a stoma formed because of malignancy means he must not donate.

question: I had a sore, red, hard vein near the surface of my leg that my GP said was a small clot. Will that stop me giving blood?
answer: Not on its own; you can donate once recovered and at least 7 days after treatment, if no other excluding factor applies.

question: I had an inflamed surface vein in my calf, stopped my ibuprofen four days ago and feel fine now. Can I donate this week?
answer: Not yet, you must wait at least 7 days after recovery and stopping treatment.

question: I'm on the waiting list for a knee replacement, which should be in about six weeks. Is it a good idea to give blood beforehand?
answer: No, donors expecting surgery within 3 months should be deferred until afterwards.

question: I had a hernia repair at a private hospital in Spain six weeks ago and I'm fully recovered. Is there a waiting period before I can donate?
answer: Yes, you must wait 3 months after surgery done outside the UK and Republic of Ireland.

question: Years ago I had the STI that gives you a painless sore and was treated with a penicillin jab. Am I able to give blood now?
answer: No, people who have had syphilis must not donate, even after treatment.

question: I was diagnosed with syphilis 15 years ago, completed treatment and the clinic says I'm cured. Can I donate?
answer: No, affected individuals must not donate; screening tests often stay positive after treatment.

question: My boyfriend has just told me he's being treated for an STI that causes a painless sore, but my own test was negative. When will I be able to give blood?
answer: After more than 3 months from your last sex with him, or more than 3 months after he finishes treatment.

question: My ex was treated for syphilis and we last slept together five weeks ago. I've never been diagnosed myself. Can I donate?
answer: No, it must be more than 3 months since your last sexual contact with the infected partner.

question: I've got tennis elbow and I'm only taking ibuprofen for it. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, if you are only taking NSAIDs you can donate.

question: My Achilles has been inflamed for a month. I'm resting it and taking naproxen, with no injections or other treatment. Is that a problem for donating whole blood?
answer: No, if the only treatment is NSAIDs you can be accepted.

question: My GP has put me on Testogel because my male hormone levels are low. Can I carry on giving blood?
answer: Yes, if it is prescribed and monitored by a UK practitioner, your haemoglobin/haematocrit is normal and the cause does not exclude you.

question: My haematocrit came back high on my testosterone injections and my GP suggested giving blood to bring it down. Will the blood service take me?
answer: No, a raised haematocrit means deferral, and donation should not be used to treat it.

question: I ended up in hospital with lockjaw after cutting myself in the garden and they gave me antibody injections. Can I give blood once I'm better?
answer: Only once fully recovered and if acceptable under the immunoglobulin therapy guidance.

question: I'm still recovering from tetanus and get stiff muscles some days. Am I allowed to donate yet?
answer: No, you must not donate until fully recovered.

question: I had my routine lockjaw booster at the GP surgery last week. Does that mean I have to wait to give blood?
answer: No, a preventive booster without an injury is acceptable.

question: I stood on a rusty nail two weeks ago and A&E gave me a tetanus immunoglobulin injection. How long before I can donate?
answer: You must wait more than 4 weeks from the injury.

question: My kids brought home worms and the whole family took the tablet from the chemist. Can I still give blood this week?
answer: Yes, you can donate even while on treatment.

question: I've got pinworms and I'm halfway through my mebendazole treatment. Do I need to postpone my donation?
answer: No, accept even if on treatment.

question: I had a clot in my leg two years ago, took blood thinners for six months and then stopped. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: Yes, for a first clot with no excluding cause and no thrombophilia, once off anticoagulants for at least 7 days.

question: I carry the Factor V Leiden gene and have never had a clot, but I was told to inject heparin before long-haul flights. Can I donate?
answer: No, people with thrombophilia who need preventive antithrombotic treatment for flights must not donate.

question: I keep getting white fungal patches on my tongue and nobody can work out why. Is it OK for me to give blood?
answer: No, unexplained oral thrush means you must not donate.

question: I developed oral thrush after a course of antibiotics and finished the miconazole gel three days ago. Can I donate today?
answer: No, you must wait 7 days after completing treatment.

question: I've got a vaginal yeast infection and I'm using Canesten cream. Can I still go and give blood?
answer: Yes, if it is not related to immunodeficiency, even while using local treatment.

question: I took a single fluconazole capsule for genital thrush four days ago. Am I able to donate yet?
answer: No, you must wait 7 days after oral (systemic) treatment.

question: I've been on the same dose of levothyroxine for years because my gland is underactive. Is that OK for giving blood?
answer: Yes, if you are on a stable dose with no changes in the last 4 weeks.

question: I took carbimazole for an overactive thyroid and stopped it 18 months ago. Am I eligible to donate now?
answer: No, you must wait 24 months after stopping anti-thyroid tablets.

question: My brother gave me one of his kidneys in 2010. Could I ever become a blood donor?
answer: No, anyone who has had a human organ transplant since 1980 must not donate.

question: I had a cornea transplant in 1975, well before the 1980 cut-off. Am I allowed to donate?
answer: No, an eye tissue transplant at any time excludes you.

question: I'm putting a prescription cream on the inside of my elbow, right where the needle would go. Does that matter?
answer: Yes, you must not donate if the needle site is affected.

question: I'm applying an antibiotic ointment to a cracked, weeping patch on the back of my hand. Can I donate this weekend?
answer: No, you must not donate with broken or infected skin.

question: I picked up a parasite from cleaning the cat's litter tray and had swollen glands for weeks. When can I give blood?
answer: Once at least 6 months have passed since you recovered.

question: I was diagnosed with toxoplasmosis and recovered three months ago. Can I donate now?
answer: No, you must wait 6 months from recovery.

question: I was given a couple of bags of blood after giving birth in 1995. Can I sign up as a donor?
answer: No, anyone who has received blood since 1 January 1980 must not donate.

question: As a child I had a transfusion in Nigeria in 1975. Is there any way I can donate?
answer: Yes, but only if a validated malaria antibody test (and T. cruzi test if relevant) is negative.

question: I was assigned male at birth and now take oestrogen as part of my transition. Am I able to give blood?
answer: Yes, if you are well, feminising hormone therapy does not stop you donating.

question: I'm non-binary and started testosterone eight months ago as part of my transition. Can I give blood yet?
answer: No, you must have been on masculinising therapy for more than 12 months.

question: I'm flying back from a long-haul holiday the day before my appointment. Is that OK?
answer: Yes, as long as you are well hydrated; delay if you are dehydrated.

question: I'm off mountaineering at high altitude in the Alps next week. Is it sensible to donate a few days before I go?
answer: It may be sensible to delay donation within 2 weeks of high-altitude exercise.

question: I had a skin prick test for TB at work and it came up as a lump. Will that stop me giving blood?
answer: Only if further investigations or treatment are planned; otherwise you can donate.

question: I had a Mantoux test last week and I'm now waiting for a follow-up chest X-ray. Can I donate in the meantime?
answer: No, not while further investigations are planned.

question: A visa health check found I carry a dormant form of the lung bug the BCG jab protects against, but I'm not on any treatment. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, people with latent TB can donate if not under investigation or treatment.

question: I finished treatment for TB in my lungs and was confirmed cured 18 months ago. Can I donate now?
answer: No, you must wait 24 months from confirmation of cure.

question: My housemate has just been diagnosed with the lung infection that the BCG protects against. Does that affect me giving blood?
answer: Yes, you must not donate until you have been screened and cleared, unless told screening isn't needed.

question: A colleague was diagnosed with TB and occupational health told me I don't need screening. Am I OK to donate?
answer: Yes, if you have been told you do not need screening, accept.

question: My daughter was born missing one of her X chromosomes but she's healthy. Can she be a blood donor?
answer: Yes, if she is in good health.

question: I have Turner syndrome, but checks show no heart or kidney problems and I feel well. Am I allowed to donate?
answer: Yes, if in good health, accept.

question: I have a permanent tube in my bladder that drains into a bag. Can I give blood?
answer: No, people with an indwelling urinary catheter must not donate.

question: I last used a tube to empty my bladder five days ago and have no signs of a water infection. Can I donate?
answer: No, it must be at least 7 days since catheterisation.

question: I've got a water infection at the moment and it stings when I wee. Should I still go to my donation appointment?
answer: No, you must not donate with an active infection.

question: I stopped taking daily Hiprex to prevent recurring bladder infections eight months ago and haven't had one since. Can I donate?
answer: No, you must wait more than 12 months after stopping preventive antiseptic therapy without recurrence.

question: I'm on Depakote for bipolar disorder. Can I give blood while I'm taking it?
answer: No, you must not donate while taking valproate.

question: I stopped topiramate for migraine prevention four days ago. How much longer do I need to wait before donating?
answer: You need more than 7 days since the last dose, provided the reason for treatment does not exclude you.

question: I've got bulging blue veins on my legs but no sores or broken skin. Does that stop me giving blood?
answer: No, they are not a reason for deferral without inflammation, clotting or ulceration.

question: I had injections to close off the veins in my leg four days ago. Can I donate this week?
answer: No, you must wait at least 7 days after sclerotherapy.

question: The room keeps spinning on me this week and I feel wobbly. Should I still give blood?
answer: No, you must not donate while having dizzy spells.

question: I have Ménière's disease and take betahistine to prevent attacks, but I feel completely fine today. Can I donate?
answer: Yes, if well on the day, even on preventive treatment.

question: I survived Ebola while working in Sierra Leone years ago. Can I give blood now?
answer: No, anyone ever diagnosed with a viral haemorrhagic fever must not donate.

question: I caught Crimean-Congo fever from a tick bite in Turkey ten years ago and recovered completely. Is there a waiting period after which I can donate?
answer: No, the deferral is permanent for anyone ever diagnosed.

question: I've just got home from a trip to a country where Lassa fever is common, and I feel fine. Do I have to wait before giving blood?
answer: Yes, you must wait 6 months from your return to the UK.

question: I nursed an Ebola patient four months ago and all my tests were negative. Can I donate yet?
answer: No, you must wait more than 6 months from last contact.

question: My husband had Ebola years ago and made a full recovery. Does that affect whether I can give blood?
answer: Yes, you must not donate if you have had sex with someone previously diagnosed.

question: Two years ago I was in a relationship with someone who had recovered from Marburg fever before we met. We've split up now. Can I donate?
answer: No, sex with someone diagnosed before your last contact means you must not donate.

question: I take a daily multi and cod liver oil capsules I buy from the chemist. Is that a problem for giving blood?
answer: No, oral self-medication is acceptable.

question: My GP prescribed high-dose folic acid last month to correct a folate deficiency. Can I give blood while I'm on it?
answer: No, you must not donate while on prescribed treatment for a deficiency.

question: I've got a verruca on my foot that I'm treating with a freezing spray. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, if there are no open wounds, even while on treatment.

question: My GP froze a wart off my finger two days ago and it's left a raw, open blister. Can I donate today?
answer: No, not while treatment has left unhealed areas.

question: I'm only seven and a half stone. Am I too light to give blood?
answer: Yes, you need to be over 50 kg (7 stone 12 pounds).

question: I weigh 67 kg and want to start doing double red cell donations. Is that heavy enough?
answer: No, double red cell donors must weigh at least 70 kg (11 stone).

question: I'm on Mounjaro jabs prescribed through an online UK pharmacy and I feel fine. Can I still give blood?
answer: Yes, if prescribed by a UK or ROI registered prescriber from a licensed source, used correctly, with no significant side effects.

question: My sister gave me a couple of her Wegovy pens to try. I don't have my own prescription. Am I allowed to donate?
answer: No, injectable medication must be prescribed for you and not shared.

question: I got back from a summer holiday where a mosquito-borne virus was going around two weeks ago, and I feel fine. Can I give blood yet?
answer: Usually you must wait 4 weeks from return, unless a validated WNV NAT test is done on the donation.

question: I had a fever and rash while in a West Nile risk area of Greece, got home three months ago and was never diagnosed. Can I donate whole blood?
answer: Only if a validated WNV NAT test is done on the donation; otherwise wait 6 months from return.

question: I only give plasma. I've just come back from somewhere with a mosquito virus outbreak — do I need to hold off?
answer: No, a plasma-only donor who is well can be accepted after returning.

question: I was diagnosed with West Nile virus in the US and I'm still tired and achy. I only donate plasma for fractionation. Can I donate?
answer: No, not until you have fully recovered.

question: I've got a small canker sore on the inside of my lip. Is that a problem for giving blood?
answer: No, small non-infected aphthous ulcers are acceptable.

question: I cut my hand gardening and it's now red, swollen and oozing pus. Can I still donate tomorrow?
answer: No, you must not donate with an infected wound.

question: As part of a research trial I was given live pig cells for my diabetes. Am I allowed to give blood?
answer: No, live animal material in contact with your blood means you must not donate.

question: I had a pig heart valve fitted years ago. Does that count as an animal transplant that would bar me from donating?
answer: No, porcine heart valves are not considered xenotransplant products.

question: My ex-husband had an experimental pig kidney put in. We split up years ago. Can I give blood?
answer: No, current or former sexual partners of xenotransplant recipients are permanently deferred.

question: My partner received live animal cells in a research trial last year and I've had no symptoms. Is there a time after which I can donate?
answer: No, the deferral for partners is permanent.

question: Years ago I was told I'd tested positive for a mouse-related virus that was supposedly linked to chronic fatigue. Can I give blood?
answer: Yes, a positive test is not a bar to donation.

question: A private clinic tested me for XMRV during my ME investigations and the result was positive. Does that stop me donating?
answer: No, donors who tested positive for XMRV are accepted.

question: I've got flu and the doctor gave me a Relenza inhaler. Can I still give blood this week?
answer: No, you must not donate while taking it as treatment for flu.

question: My son has flu, so the GP gave me Relenza as a precaution. I've had no symptoms and wasn't told to stay at home. Can I donate?
answer: Yes, if taking it as prevention with no flu symptoms and not advised to stay home.
